o: Given s with all-distinct characters and t a permutation of s, sum |index_in_s(c) − index_in_t(c)| over all characters c. For s='abc', t='bac': |0−1|+|1−0|+|2−2| = 2. For s='abcde', t='edbac': the six pairwise contributions sum to 12. Since each character appears once in each string, a single hash map from character to its index in s, then one pass over t, computes the answer in linear time. Length ≤ 26 means even quadratic scanning would pass, but the map is the clean solution.
k: Build pos[c] = index of c in s once; then the answer is Σ |pos[t[i]] − i| over i.
No sorting or extra structures needed — one map and one pass.

a.i: Record each character's index in s in a dictionary. Iterate t with its index i and accumulate the absolute difference against pos[t[i]]. Every character of t is guaranteed present in the map since t is a permutation of s.
s: Create pos mapping each s[i] to i.
Loop over t with index i, adding abs(pos[t[i]] − i) to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build the map, one pass to accumulate.
a.sp: O(1) — the map/array holds at most 26 entries.

a.i: Because n ≤ 26, for each character of t we can simply scan s for its index with indexOf/str.find. Quadratic in principle but constant-bounded here; it avoids any auxiliary structure and is the shortest possible code.
s: For each index i of t, find j = s.indexOf(t[i]).
a.t: O(n²) worst case, but n ≤ 26 makes it effectively constant.

w: Use the hash-map version — it is linear and generalizes to strings with repeated characters (map from character to a list of positions, matched in order). Pitfalls: none serious; just ensure absolute values and remember t is guaranteed to be a permutation so lookups never miss. Follow-ups: define the difference with squared distances, or compute it between two permutations of a multiset where stable matching of duplicates is required.
